desc:
An undirected graph has n nodes labelled 0 to n - 1 and the connections listed in edges, where edges[i] = [a, b] joins a and b. The graph may consist of several separate pieces.

You want to delete some connections so that no cycle remains anywhere in the graph (the result must be a forest: every piece is a tree). Return the smallest number of connections you have to delete. Deleting a connection never deletes a node.
constraints: No two edges join the same pair of nodes
hints: A graph with no cycles has a very specific number of edges for a given number of nodes and pieces. What is it?
A forest with n nodes and c connected pieces has exactly n - c edges.

You can keep at most n - c edges, where c is the number of components of the original graph (deleting edges never merges pieces, and a spanning forest keeps every piece connected). So the answer is m - (n - c).
editorial: Deleting edges can only keep the number of pieces the same or increase it, and a forest on n nodes with c pieces has exactly n - c edges. The best you can do is keep a spanning tree of each component, which uses n - c edges in total, where c is the number of components of the original graph. Everything else has to go, so the answer is m - n + c.

So the whole task reduces to counting connected components with a DFS, BFS or union-find, in O(n + m) time. The value m - n + c is known as the cyclomatic number of the graph: the number of independent cycles. A union-find that counts how many edges join two nodes that were already connected gives the same number.
